newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn retreats in gold showdown, says will make EMU.
newsitem.headline: Bonn retreats in gold showdown, says will make EMU.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government retreated on Tuesday from a controversial plan to revalue Bundesbank gold reserves, but Finance Minister Theo Waigel said Germany would still qualify for Europe's single currency.

Waigel, speaking after coalition deputies baulked at his unpopular grab for gold, told journalists he and the central bank president Hans Tietmeyer had reached "a good compromise" that would transfer windfall profits to Bonn only next year.

The minister, hectically seeking 19 billion marks ($11 billion) to make up for his 1997 revenue shortfalls, told Christian Democrat deputies in a closed-door meeting he had to cut spending and speed up privatisations to meet the Maastricht criteria.
"We will manage it in 1997," he told reporters afterwards.

Bank analysts said the Frankfurt-based Bundesbank had won the unprecedented showdown and would now keep an eagle eye on Bonn to make sure it did not weaken the Maastricht criteria or agree with the new Socialist government in France to widen the first group of countries in the monetary union (EMU) in 1999.
"The Bundesbank is clearly the one that has come out on top of this," Ros Lifton, senior international economist at HSBC Markets in London.

The humbling climbdown ended a six-day showdown between Kohl's hamstrung government and the powerful central bank, whose thundering rejection of any quick grab at its undervalued gold set off a major power struggle between Kohl and Tietmeyer.
But it did not end Waigel's drawn-out budget woes because he said he might still need to raise taxes, a move coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP) have vehemently opposed.

Deputies said Kohl threw his weight squarely behind Waigel and vowed to rebuff all critics in parliament when the minister speaks on Wednesday. One deputy said Kohl admitted that he shared responsibility for the budget problem, which has led to the biggest challenge to his government in 14 years.
"We are in a difficult situation. It would be absurd (not to say so)," CDU parliamentary leader Wolfgang Schaeuble said.
FDP leader Wolfgang Gerhardt echoed Waigel's determination to meet the three percent deficit-to-GDP Maastricht target but insisted it had to be done without tax hikes.
"I think we can and should meet the criteria and solve the budget problem without tax increases," he said.
Waigel gave no details of the gold compromise but FDP parliamentary leader Hermann Otto Solms said only the Bundesbank's currency reserves would be revalued now.
"That would mean that the currency reserves are revalued in this year, and then the corresponding profits can follow next year," he said.
The gold deal emerged after Waigel and Tietmeyer met in Bonn for what was to be secret talks. Scores of journalists appeared at the Finance Ministry once word spread.

"We had good talks and we are on the way to an agreement," Waigel said. "We are indeed," Tietmeyer added after short meeting. "I hope that we can come to an agreement." They declined to provide further details and walked quickly away.

The central bank was not in principle opposed to revaluing its gold reserves but insisted that the process should not take place until 1999, or at least not before the decision as to who will participate in monetary union, in May 1998.
The Bundesbank has some 95 million ounces of gold in its reserves, valued at 13.7 billion marks compared to a current market value of more than 55 billion marks.

The government's unprecedented grab for the gold raised eyebrows throughout Europe, especially in countries where German officials had long been delivering stern lectures against such budgetary sleight-of-hand.
Parliamentary deputies in Kohl's CDU and Waigel's Christian Social Union (CSU) pressed them to back down or face possible defeat in voting over the plan.
Michael Glos, head of the CSU parliamentary group, explained the retreat by saying differences between the Bundesbank and the government had been too small to fight over.
"A public dispute is not worth it either for the Bundesbank or for the government," he said. "We have a saying -- the smarter one backs down." ($ = 1.727 German Marks)
